before: The Creator.

For there is one God, the Father, from whom all things proceed, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made; and again, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever, into the ages. How then can he be the same as he was yesterday, even though he was born in the most recent times of this age? It is because the most ancient nature of the Word of God has remained necessarily unshakeable, even during the era of the incarnation and this most recent dispensation.

Indeed, he at times used words concerning the forefather Abraham to address Israel, saying, "Your father Abraham rejoiced so that he might see my day, and he saw it and was glad" (John 8:56). But those who did not understand the mystery resting upon him—viewing him merely as a man like ourselves and nothing more—incoherently asked, "Do you not yet have fifty years, and you have seen Abraham?" (John 8:57). But he said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:56-58). Therefore, he is the artisan and the creator of both Abraham and Moses and of all things; and it is necessary that the maker pre-announce all his own works, and that the beauty of the archetype be pre-manifested in those created according to his image.
In this way, the measure of Moses is unequally surpassed; rather, the glory of Christ will exceed all that has been called into existence.
Furthermore, by another method, the lawgiver Paul seeks to demonstrate that the word concerning these matters has become both wise and true.
For he says that Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant for the testimony of the things to be spoken, but Christ is as a Son upon his house, which is the house of whom we are.
So look, then, in order that you might assign to the blessed Moses a certain measure of that householder-like genuineness.
For they say that he is to be in the house faithful as a witness of the things to be spoken—that is, for the service of the words from God—but Christ is not so.

For He is not [found] as a faithful householder in the house, but as Son and Master over the house of the Father; that is to say, over us, the ones having been justified in faith and sanctified in the Spirit.

For Moses indeed was brought up through the shadow of the law, and the qualities of householder-like genuineness were brought to him as a prize, as God was saying to him, 'You shall stand beside him with me' (Hebrews 3:5), and he was greatly esteemed among the better ones in Christ.
For He has sat 'at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the high places' (Hebrews 1:3), and He has dwelt as Son and Lord in the house of His own Father.

For He encamps for us as God through His own Spirit, even though the all-wise Moses inhabited in nothing; for we have not become partakers of Moses, nor even of any other of the saints, but we have partaken of Christ through the Spirit and the blessing of the mystery.
For even though God says through one of the holy prophets, 'I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be a people to me' (Ezekiel 37:27).

before: …That is, from the earth; a staining of garments from Bosporus?"—a term which in the Greek tongue signifies compression or affliction—"that your garments and your clothing are red, as if from the tread of a winepress?" They were approaching him there, saying, "What are these wounds which are in the midst of your hands?" And he replied to them, "As I was struck in my beloved house." No one would have clearly asserted that it was necessary for him to retain the marks of the nails after the resurrection and to ascend into heaven with them.
It is more worthy to contemplate that matter.

Just as he showed the side to the unbelieving Thomas, along with the marks of the nails, so that he might finally believe and say with a learning mind, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), so also he appeared through the signs of the passion, making the manner of the economy after the flesh manifest to the holy angels. Indeed, he bore red garments and the marks of the nails so that they too might believe that, being by nature and truly existing God, he had become a son of man, having taken a body from the holy Virgin and having seated himself in self-emptying, so that, having offered himself as a sacrifice and a victim for all as a fragrance of sweetness to God and the Father, he might save those under heaven.

The holy multitude of the angels also worships him. They do not refuse this worship because he was a firstborn and a man among many brothers, but having been taught the economy, they recognize the Son from God according to nature and the moment when he became flesh.
…But to the Son: "Your throne, O God" (Psalm 45:7).

How, then, is it not foolish and impudent to scrutinize that nature through which all things were provided toward existence, a nature older than all time? For through it the Word has come to be, and before all ages, the Word is from God the Father.
Yet the wanderers accuse him of being recent, claiming that he is a created being, not realizing that they are opposing the words of the Holy Spirit.
For those who speak in the Spirit say that the ages were made through him.
But those who insist he is a created being base their argument on what lies beyond intellect and reason, failing to grasp even that through the lens of intellect.
For God did not become Father within time, but he was always so, even in the beginning.
Since this is the case, it is a necessity in every respect to conceive of the Son as co-existing, so that God may truly be called Father.

Since they have taught that if the Son is the Word of the Father, and wisdom, and power, and the character and radiance of his subsistence, then what sort of time was it during which the Father was without the Logos, lacking the Son? When was the source of wisdom without wisdom itself? When was power without its power? When was the radiance of his glory not present in God? Or how could his own character not be continuously with him and in him? If indeed these things came to pass within time, then he was not Father before he was begotten; he would have been without Logos, without wisdom, and without strength, lacking both character and radiance.
But I consider it impious to conceive of such a thing, and it is the highest impiety…

before: The tabernacle had three sections: the altar, the middle section where the priests performed their daily services after passing through the veil, and the innermost section.
This middle section was called the Holy Place, and it was here that the priests would enter to perform their services, which were a type of the old covenant, where the blood sacrifices were offered.
The innermost section was known as the Holy of Holies, which was a type of the mystery among us.
The apostle Paul refers to the first tabernacle, located after the bronze altar, as being towards the Holy of Holies, since it was in the middle, separated from the court by the veil.
After the middle tabernacle, there was another veil, and behind this veil was the Holy of Holies, into which no one entered except the high priest, and he only once a year.

Inside the Holy of Holies was the ark of the covenant, which contained the tablets of the law, the jar of manna, and Aaron's rod; however, some traditions say that only the tablets were placed in the ark, but Paul may have added the rod and jar from tradition.
Above the ark were the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat.
The prophet declares that he was shown to us, 'when he saw the glory, and spoke about it' (Isaiah 6:1-3).

For he says, 'I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a high and exalted throne' (Isaiah 6:1), and the seraphim stood around him, and the Lord on the throne was glorified, stretching out their wings, and they glorified him.
Thus it was arranged and in the holy tabernacle the cherubim with their wings overshadowing the mercy seat.
If the golden cherubim had a voice, they would have glorified the Lord Sabaoth, the Son of God who appeared in the form of a servant, the only begotten from God the Father according to nature.
The Spirit of grace was insulted.
Various baptisms and ordinances of the flesh were in place until the time of correction, but they were limited in their ability to perfect anyone in conscience.

The law introduced teachings of baptisms and narratives of purifications for the cleanliness of the flesh, but these were merely fleshly commandments, justifying those who seemed unclean according to the flesh.
Even if someone touched a dead person or a leper or became unclean, they would be baptized and thus seemed to be cleansed.

God did not allow those from the blood of Israel to dwell among the shadows of the law, for He commanded the lamb to be sacrificed as a type of Christ, signifying that the things in types would not stand forever, but would run towards the truth (Exodus 12:1-28).

Consider how the mercy seat was made into an image of the Son who became human; for then it became a mercy seat; but the cherubim were commanded to stand around and overshadow with their wings, always turned towards and looking at him.

before: …It seems to think outside the gate, outside the world; for wanting to follow Christ unsettles our worldly life.

But the one who does good and is in communion is accepted by God, who rewards each according to their works, and says, 'Come, inherit the kingdom prepared for you, for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat' (Matt 25:34-35), and the following, how God is thus called by the pure voice of the saints, while accepting the sacrifices of those who do good, repaying each with the due reward, and admitting the chorus of the saints into the kingdom of heaven.

Paul calls the Son God; for if He is indeed the one who drives all creation toward judgment, and repays each according to their works, accepting those who do good to their neighbor and saying, 'Come, inherit the kingdom prepared for you, for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat' (Matt 25:34-35).

If it were said that the only-begotten Word of God happened to be united to the flesh by hypostasis, we do not say that any confusion of the two natures has occurred, but rather that the Word is understood to be united to the flesh while the other remains as it is.

'Those who think themselves wise have become foolish' (1 Cor 3:19); for they, having denied the two natures from one another and showing each part of us to be an incompatible stranger, say that the union exists only in persons, as if it were in mere agreement, common purpose, and the impulses of wills.

According to that, perhaps, what is written in the acts of the holy apostles (Acts 4:32), that 'the heart and the soul of the multitude of those who believed were one.' For each of those who believed, insofar as they were divided from the others by the logic of their own hypostasis, yet reached a common purpose and unity of faith, is said to have one soul and one heart; do they, then, acknowledge the unity of persons in this same way?
And not yet do we say that the nature of the Word of God is circumscribed in the human body, for the divine is incomprehensible.

Furthermore, it proceeds: one will see the human being completely in Christ, according to the logic of His own nature; and similarly, the Word born from God is seen as perfect; yet only one Christ and Son is confessed from both…

before: He has declared concerning us at times, 'I will proclaim your name to my brothers,' and at other times, 'Behold, I and the children which God gave to me' (Ps 27:10; Ps 68:5). For all things are being handed over to him by God and the Father, and we have become his inheritance, even though we were formerly like portions of foxes, as David says.
For we the cowardly lie underneath the herds of the demons.
But Christ slew all of us with his own blood and has inherited.

And indeed he spoke toward the Father and God in the heavens, 'Those whom you gave to me out of the world were yours, and you gave them to me, and the glory which you gave to me, I have given to them' (John 17:6, 10). For even though he is Son by nature, he says that through the human he partook of such glory by grace with us, while having remained what he had given to us, his own glory.

For he sealed us with his own Spirit toward adoption, and in him we cry, 'Abba, Father' (Rom 8:15). Do we not, we who are numbered among children, partake of God in blood and flesh—that is, we are in blood and in flesh, and in corruptible and earthly bodies?

Because of this cause, the Only-begotten Word of God, being life by nature, partook of these same things, and not by any other way but similarly, in order that he might abolish the one having power over death.

Because it was not possible for that which is overcome by death, corruption, and sin to be brought back to its beginning except through Christ alone—the mystery of the incarnation to be fulfilled in its appointed time—the blessed David exhorted us, saying: 'Why, Lord, have you set me far off, and do you look on in times of trouble?' (Psalm 21:13). This is why he is called Emmanuel.
For he has not set us far off any longer, but the Word of God, having become man, has indeed become nearer to us.

In a similar way he partook of blood and flesh for our sake; for the human race upon the earth is ruled by death and corruption. It seemed good to God, the All, through great gentleness and philanthropy, to 'recapitulate' all things in Christ (1 Cor 15:22), so that death might be rendered powerless and, just as it was in the first Christ, those overcoming in their earthly bodies might find life.

Thus, the power of incorruption is being extended into our entire race. The divine Paul will be believed when he writes: 'For through man came death, and through man the resurrection of the dead' (1 Cor 15:22). It was necessary that the one who suffered be healed, and that death be abolished through the flesh which is tyrannized by death.

Just as in Adam, having stumbled through transgression, humanity fell under death, so too, because he became well-pleasing in Christ through obedience, the yokes of death are torn away and its terrors are scattered. As they spring upon us, he cries out: 'O Death, where is your victory? O Hades, where is your sting?' (1 Cor 15:55). For the Only-begotten Word of God, existing as life, essentially joined himself to the earth and died in the flesh, so that even to him, just as to one of the unhonored...

before: Having sinned through Adam's transgression, humanity is shown to be in need of restoration, so that the one who enriches us may again be revealed. For the Word, being God by nature, humbled himself and became human, a little lower than the angels, to restore humanity to glory and honor. "We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because he suffered death" (Hebrews 2:9).

If someone says that the man born of the Virgin is worthy of memory and care from God, they will bring shame, for where is Christ as a mere human, and when is he thought of without the united Word? How then can he be said to be worthy of care and memory from God?

The Lord is one, and our faith is one, and we have one baptism. Although the difference between natures is significant, the mode of union has revealed one Son from both. If we are worthy of memory from God the Word, then we are certainly psychic, lacking the spirit as it is written (1 Corinthians 14:14). We divide the one into two.

The body of the Word is not foreign to the Word itself. If the one born from the holy virgin has undergone emptying, how can he be emptied if he is glorified? Is it not an honor and glory for a human to be deemed worthy of oversight and memory, and to attain union with God? If they say that the emptying was done to the Monogenes, then he has been emptied by having suffered. For the one to whom suffering has happened, it is fitting that the matter of emptying has also happened.

Christ, as God, is deemed worthy of memory from God and has become one of the beneficiaries, and we approach Him as God in prayer, requesting the supply of heavenly goods, as He distributes the requests to all creation in a God-pleasing manner. This is evident because the children have shared in blood and flesh, and Christ has similarly shared in these things.

It is necessary to carefully examine which children the word is about, who have shared in flesh and blood, and how Christ has similarly participated in these things. When the Only-Begotten Word of God, being God and Lord by nature and co-throned with God the Father, was measured to the level of humanity, He was composed as a brother to those called through faith to the adoption of God. Then the economy's cleverness is well done.

If the Only-begotten Word of God had not become man, and had instead assumed the human countenance unto himself—as those who discern [the mystery] seem to suggest, that it occurred through good-will alone or by a mere inclination of will—how could he have been made like his brothers in all things? Furthermore, how could anyone fully conceive of him as a brother, when he is the one who transcends all, surpassing those incomparable excellencies which I call natural, and surpassing even creation? How could he have shared in blood and flesh unless these things had become his own, just as they are ours? Thus, there is truly one Son and Lord, having been joined in unity of subsistence through the Word's participation in human flesh and blood and having been made like his brothers in every respect.
This was so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest.

Moses, the divinely inspired lawgiver, came to bring Israel into the knowledge of God through type and shadow, and showed the way of righteousness through the law; yet he was slow of voice and slow of tongue.
Because of this, the God of all was known even to those in Judah alone, from Dan even unto Beersheba, and by the river and the sea.
For these are the boundaries of the land of the Jews.
And his name was great and most widely known.

I say that he names the land of promise everywhere.

But our Lord Jesus Christ has become a merciful and faithful High Priest for the propitiation of the sins of the people, and in Him, having been tested, He was helped by those who are being tested.

For He has called the inhabited world to a holy and heavenly calling, and He has become High Priest; for He was not a minister of the law that condemns, but rather, through forgetfulness and by grace and love, He has justified through faith and has granted us the washing of the ancient sins.

For being both always and by nature merciful, His only-begotten Word has been set as our mediator and the mediator of God through the Incarnation, so that just as He was always kind and merciful, so indeed, having been shown as High Priest again, He dwells among those on the earth, acting as a friend to those who are beloved by Him and not departing from His own…

before: It has proof. He was always the Father, and therefore the Son also existed, coexisting eternally with his own begetter.
You loved righteousness.

The divine David, addressing the Father in heaven and God as if with a voice common to all humanity, cried out this prayer: 'God, command by your power, strengthen,' and 'God accomplishes what he has worked in us.' (Psalm 67:30)
But the power of the Father is the Son, through whom he made the heavens firm and established the earth, and has brought about the adornment of this world.
Moreover, he made man according to his own image and likeness, a worker of righteousness who surpasses corruption and death.

Yet because death has reigned through sin and we have become subject to corruption, and 'all have gone astray, together become useless,' the Maker and Lord of all things necessarily foresaw this among his own creations.
For God and Father was pleased to sum up all things in Christ and to renew them to their original state.

Therefore David, penetrating the deep mystery of the incarnation, proclaims to the Son who is from God by nature: 'You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore, God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.' (Psalm 44:7-8)
Some think these words do not belong to the Only-begotten but should rather be spoken to a mere man, the one begotten from the holy virgin.
Yet such thinking is foolish, as demonstrated by many arguments.

It was not an ordinary man who was born to us, merely sharing our nature but stripped of any true unity with God, so that one might claim, following their own reasoning, to have foreknown him—the God of all things—as one who loves righteousness and hates lawlessness based solely on a private opinion.
Yet we may fittingly apply the voice of the Psalmist to the Only-Begotten who has appeared in human form, and direct our attention to Isaiah’s prophecies concerning him.
For he declared: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.' (Isaiah 7:14)
He shall eat butter and honey before he knows how to refuse evil and choose the good.

For before the child knows either good or evil, he refuses wickedness in order to choose the good; he has loved righteousness and hated iniquity by his very nature, being righteousness and God himself.

For as yet, from the time of his birth, the child does not know what is hardened, nor does he praise what is not so constituted; how then could he have disobeyed wickedness in order to choose the good?
But he was, as I have said, God in the flesh—those naturally good things which belong to him being carried forth outside himself.

I do not merely praise what I wish to say; let it stand if it seems right according to the reasoning of the envious and the special virtue of one who dwells in face-to-face union and has been honored.

But since they say these things, I will ask: From what works then will this one be such—and yet, being a man according to nature, just as those of the divine order—be deemed worthy to receive thrones, to sit in counsel with God and the Father, and to be proclaimed Lord, equal with the One who is according to nature?

before: Through the good-will of God and the Father, we are enriched in our supernatural nature by being in Christ, who raised us up and seated us in the heavenly places (Psalm 8:4-6).
For because He, the Savior of us all, is seated, He surpasses the whole boast of human nature.
We have become rich through Christ's poverty, but only if we are superior to all creation, for it is through His humility that we are exalted.

Therefore, let man be diminished a little from the angels, having become such, so that he might honor the human nature and recover it again to its original state, in glory and honor, being crowned in it, even though he is a lord of glory as God.

Just as the transgression of Adam demonstrated the most dishonorable state, so shall we be glorified through the obedience of Christ on our behalf, He having set forth His own soul so that He might rule both over the dead and the living (Psalm 8:4-6).
How is Christ diminished from the angels, He who is worshiped among them? It is because He sat within the measures of humanity; having received a body destined to die, He willingly suffered in it.
Yet through Him, having abolished death and rendered corruption inactive, He is crowned with the highest glories, being incorruption and life.
As for the things of superiority, they belong to the angels, for they are better off outside of flesh and of death, it having happened in these things of the Son through His voluntary emptying.

But Christ, though briefly diminished from the angels because of the measure of humanity, is worshiped by them in the excellence of His divinity; He is established upon thrones, which those standing around Him always glorify, calling Him Lord by the powers.
That He might taste death above all by the grace of God (Hebrews 2:9).
For as I think, what it means to have 'tasted all' is clear, as it is written, 'That he might taste death above all by the grace of God' (Hebrews 2:9).
For having given His own body to death, and as if having fleshly tasted that which occurred, He lived again and has immediately trampled the power of death.

Therefore, the One said to be briefly diminished from the angels is the Word who is from God; He did not suffer this diminishment into His own nature, for He is always the same, possessing the same nature, unshakeable and unchangeable, yet He has endured this also through us in a human way.

For He was sustaining Himself, even though by nature He is God, according to the measures of humanity because of the divine economy, and this is part of the mystery according to Him, that it is most proper to marvel at.

So also the prophet Habakkuk said, 'Lord, I have heard the sound of your hearing and I was afraid, I understood your works and was astonished' (Habakkuk 3:2), for truly, what has happened is an ecstasy and a wonder beyond all.

But I do not know how some, not having understood the mystery correctly, vaunt themselves and desire to interpret what is written in the eighth psalm, specifically the verse 'What is man, that you remember him, or a son of man, that you visit him?' (Psalm 8:4).

Let us therefore observe what kind of man it is that causes one to be struck with wonder, marveling that the Only-begotten was indeed worthy to be remembered by him and to have performed an inspection, as it is written, 'What is man, that you remember him, or a son of man, that you visit him?' (Psalm 8:4).

He proceeds from this to argue most clearly, as if the following had never been said of any man, that the blessed Paul, speaking of his own person, applied the words of the Psalm, saying 'made a little lower than the angels' (Psalm 8:5), we see Jesus being crowned with 'glory and honor' through the passion of death.

Furthermore, by distinguishing between natures, they claim privately that the man born of the Holy Virgin is a man of a strange sort; regarding this, they say that David marvels that he was worthy of both remembrance and visitation, and that he was worthy also of a unique nature above nature, as one receiving benefit from the Divine Word.

But they have failed to understand, as it appears, that Christ Jesus is not a man in Himself, understood and spoken of among us in a common or private sense; rather, it is the Word from God who has become man, and in order that the expression of the concepts may be properly understood…
The prophet David says, 'You have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor' (Psalm 8:5), and 'You have put all things under his feet' (Psalm 8:6).

before: As the world unfolds in the necessary world, the wonder of Christ's name becomes apparent, and it is worth considering the theory presented in the psalm that has been placed before us.

The prophet David knew that according to the true and divine promise, Christ would be born from the fruit of his loins, and God, existing by nature, would sit among us in due time, speaking in the eighth psalm and making words to him as to a human and also to God, recognizing the one God from both.
He says, 'Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth, for your magnificence has been lifted up above the heavens' (Psalm 8:1).
For where or among whom is Christ not wondered at, or how has his magnificence not been lifted up above the heavens?

If it is true that in the name of Jesus Christ every knee bends and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10-11), then it is clear that Christ's name is indeed wonderful and his magnificence has been lifted up above the heavens.

When Christ raised Lazarus from the dead, all were amazed, and as he sat on a donkey, children waved palm branches and cried out 'Hosanna to the son of David, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Matthew 21:9).
The others rebuked them, but Christ said, 'Have you not read that I will perfect praise from the mouth of infants and sucklings?' (Matthew 21:16).

This event shows that even though Christ is God by nature, he humbled himself to such an extent that he allowed himself to be led by the crowd, and Paul declares that he has been stripped of the former glory, saying he has been stripped of it.
The blessed David saw the reason for this emptying and understood that it was so that Christ might rescue us from corruption and sin and the tyrannical hands of the devil.
The mystery of the economy with flesh is worthy of all wonder.
He says, 'Lord, what is man that you remember him, or the son of man that you visit him?' (Psalm 8:4).
For what is human nature in relation to God, and what is this that I say, what is human genus?
What portion is assigned to them on earth in relation to the orders of holy angels?
Even if man is nothing by nature and number, the Creator did not despise us, for he remembered us and deemed us worthy of visitation, as if we were perishing.

In the beginning, God brought us into existence, lowering us briefly below the angels, but then crowning us with honor and glory, setting us over the works of his hands, and subjecting all things under our feet.

The divine Paul skillfully sets forth the things concerning us, which have been renewed through Christ, and the scope of the whole song is in these things, appearing in the necessary world as it unfolds.
The things in Christ are a new creation, and the old things have passed away, and all things have become new.
The Holy Spirit says through one of the prophets, 'Take courage, Zion, do not let your hands weaken; the Lord your God is in you, to save you and renew you in his love' (Isaiah 41:10).
Paul declares us to be stripped of the former glory, and therefore, he says, 'Now we do not yet see all things subjected to him' (1 Corinthians 15:28).

before: The Word from God the Father would not reasonably decline His own things, for if considered in Himself, He is in need of no good, and the Holy Spirit is said to be His own. Since, as I said, He became flesh with His own Spirit, anointing His own temple, the Father works all things through the Son alone in Israel. The Spirit is said to be received economically, as a man, for it is said that Jesus from Nazareth was anointed by God with the Holy Spirit and power (Luke 4:18).

But as God, He gives the Spirit to those worthy to receive it, and indeed, He breathed on the holy apostles, saying 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22). The divine Peter proclaimed to the Jewish crowds concerning the Spirit, saying that Jesus, having been exalted to the right hand of God, received the promise of the Spirit from the Father and poured it out (Acts 2:33). You hear in these words that He was exalted to the right hand of God, received and gave the Spirit; He was exalted, of course, when He humbled Himself. Just as He willingly humbled Himself for this purpose, so again He exalts Himself, being the hand of the Father by which all things are worked in a godly manner. He is exalted through Himself according to the will of the Father, when, having broken the bonds of death and having said to the spirits below 'Come out' (Luke 23:43), He sat at the right hand of the Father.

When Jesus said to his apostles, 'I am going to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God' (John 20:17), he clearly referred to his own Father as God, speaking from his human perspective. Through him, we have been called to adoption, and he has given us his Father as our own. Just as we, though called sons of the Father, are still human and have not forgotten the grace of the one who honored us, so too the natural Son and Lord, though he recognized God as his Father through his flesh and his likeness to us, did not cease to be what he is.

The Word of God, who became human through us, anoints his own temple with his own Spirit, not imparting a partial energy, nor in a hierarchical order as he gives to us, but rather filling it with sanctification and his own power and glory. For he said, 'I sanctify myself for their sake, so that they also may be' (John 17:19). We, on the other hand, have been anointed with the Holy Spirit, and by nature, we have been defined as being such, to the extent that the nature of divinity of all created things is understood. How then can it be said that he was anointed apart from those who share in him? Let us consider this question and try to provide an answer.
